All three source subquestions are grouped to avoid counting nested parameter variants separately. The direction quantifier for theta_mu must be resolved from the model before a theorem claim.

For a straight test ray segment of length L in direction alpha and mirrors of total length epsilon with orientation law mu, the centers whose mirror crosses the segment form a parallelogram of area epsilon L |sin(alpha-beta)| for angle beta. M>=2 is needed for the matrix size to be meaningful. The two clauses are retained as one source conjecture, not counted twice.

For M=2 the matrix has three complex Gaussian rows. Almost surely these span C^2. The real-linear measurement map from the four-dimensional Hermitian 2-by-2 space to R^3 has a nonzero kernel element H. H cannot be positive or negative semidefinite: a_i^* H a_i=0 for a spanning set would force H=0. Thus H has one positive and one negative eigenvalue and can be written xx^*-yy^* with noncollinear x,y. Their three intensity measurements agree. Hence p_2=0.

Dimension gives a nonzero H without assuming generic rank three; the spanning condition rules out semidefinite kernel elements. Spectral decomposition independently verifies equal squared magnitudes.

For M>2 a nonzero kernel matrix need not have rank at most two with one eigenvalue of each sign. The requisite low-rank intersection probability remains unresolved.

# P0016  Worst square-submatrix conditioning in a Gaussian frame

Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025; Open Problem 21 and Definition 10.1, Entry 10

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.29571

Source statement date: not established. Archived access: 2026-09-06T15:32:10Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

For a (2M-1)-by-M matrix of independent standard real Gaussians, determine the asymptotic size of omega(A), the minimum smallest singular value over row subsets whose complement has rank below M. In particular determine whether its decay is exponential and identify the exponential rate.

Almost surely every M-row subset is nonsingular, so the minimum reduces to M-row subsets. Interpret asymptotic size in probability; the source does not specify a convergence mode or a normalized logarithmic limit.

For a standard M-by-M real Gaussian matrix A, sigma_min(A)<=t implies that some column has distance at most sqrt(M)t from the span of the other columns: project a minimizing unit vector equation using a coordinate of magnitude at least 1/sqrt(M). Each such distance has the law |N(0,1)|, so P(sigma_min<=t)<=sqrt(2/pi) M^(3/2)t. There are at most 4^M M-row submatrices of a (2M-1)-by-M frame. Therefore its minimum omega exceeds exp(-(log 4+epsilon)M) with probability tending to one. Conversely fix M-1 rows and a unit normal u. The M remaining row projections are independent N(0,1), and omega is at most their minimum absolute value, giving omega<=C log(M)/M with probability tending to one for sufficiently large C.

Full spark holds almost surely. Adding rows increases the Gram matrix, so the minimum relevant frame bound is attained among M-row subsets. Both bounds use union/inclusion inequalities and never assume independence among overlapping minors.

The exponential lower bound and polynomial upper bound are far apart. Sharp extremes of the strongly dependent minors remain uncontrolled.

# P0028  Bounded independent Brownian pieces and two-sided Brownian motion

Krzysztof Burdzy: My favorite open problems; Problem 8; compare Burdzy-Scheutzow (2014) Problem 7.7

https://sites.math.washington.edu/~burdzy/open_mathjax.php

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Concatenate independent Brownian path segments cut at stopping times indexed by all integers, with lengths uniformly bounded by a deterministic constant and divergent sums in both directions. Is the resulting path two-sided Brownian after some random time shift?

The paper's related backward-Brownian question and its almost-sure random bound are recorded as related variants, not an extra count. Independent lengths alone are not the same as stopping times depending on their Brownian paths.

For iid stopped Brownian segments with 0<E T<infinity, the cycle sequence is ergodic under shifting its index. A stationary occupation law is Q(F)=E[integral_0^T F(theta_s X) ds]/E T. Shifting by t changes the numerator by E[integral_T^(T+t) F(theta_s X) ds-integral_0^t F(theta_s X) ds]=0 because the concatenation rooted at the next cycle has the same Palm law. Tilting the iid cycle sequence by T_0/E T and choosing a uniform time in that cycle realizes this law; the forward filling lemma supplies that tilt by a finite randomized index shift.

For each deterministic s, {s<T} is measurable from the segment up to s. Future Brownian increments followed by independent stopped segments retain the Brownian law and are independent of the past. Integrating over s gives a Brownian future under Q; stationarity then supplies a Brownian past and its independence. This is a proof outline pending full artifact and earlier-literature comparison, not a newly claimed theorem.

The actual question allows independent non-identically distributed segments. There is then no invariant iid index law or common Palm mean to which this argument applies.

On the 2-by-2 grid (a four-cycle), exactly two peaks must be opposite and carry labels 3 and 4. There are two choices of diagonal, two orders of the top labels, and two orders of the bottom labels: eight of the 24 labelings. Their graph distance is always two. The source indexing omits the first step; use its intended new-site rule also at time zero. The analogous four- and three-dimensional results do not decide this planar model.

The axis of the next step is predictable from the past, while its sign is fair. Both coordinates are martingales, their cross quadratic covariation is zero, and E|X_n|^2=n. Bounded increments and Azuma give summable bounds for P(|X_n|>epsilon n), so X_n/n tends to zero almost surely.

The predictable quadratic variation of the horizontal coordinate counts first visits, and the vertical one counts repeat visits; their sum is exactly n.

If T is any geodesic spanning tree rooted at the identity of a Cayley graph of growth rate b, must br(T)=b, equivalently must its Bernoulli bond percolation threshold be 1/b?

The branching-number/percolation equivalence is a theorem of the source. The question is stated there geometrically; its probability formulation is recorded transparently. Lexicographically minimal spanning trees satisfy it.

A geodesic spanning tree has exactly the Cayley graph sphere sizes at each level. But growth can exceed branching number for a bounded-degree tree: take a single infinite spine and at its nth vertex attach a finite b-ary tree of height n. Its level sizes have exponential rate sqrt(b)>1, while its only infinite ray is the spine and arbitrarily deep singleton cutsets give branching number one.

At level m the largest attached contribution starts around n=m/2 and has order b^(m/2), up to constant factors and a geometric sum. Every attachment is finite, so no additional infinite ray appears.

This is not a geodesic Cayley spanning-tree counterexample. It proves that matching sphere counts alone cannot establish the conjectured branching number.

Use graph distance in the cluster for the cluster speed as in the source context; compare with ambient speed carefully. Nonamenable cases are reported known.

Let H be a connected subgraph of a bounded-degree graph G with |B_G(x,n)|=exp(o(n)). The Carne-Varopoulos bound gives P_x(X_n=y)<=2 sqrt(deg_H(y)/deg_H(x)) exp(-d_H(x,y)^2/(2n)). Summing over reachable vertices yields P(d_H(x,X_n)>=epsilon n)<=C exp(o(n)-epsilon^2 n/2), which is summable. Thus the intrinsic speed on H is zero almost surely.

Reachability in H implies membership in B_G(x,n), but distances in the exponential bound remain intrinsic to H. Bounded degrees control the prefactor. This is a consequence of the classical heat-kernel bound, not a novelty claim.

It settles the zero-speed equivalence for subexponential-growth Cayley graphs and their clusters only. Exponential-growth cases need different information.

Is a finitely generated group amenable exactly when every Cayley graph from every finite generating set has bootstrap complete-occupation critical probability p(G,k) in {0,1} for every threshold k?

Initially each vertex is occupied independently with probability p; vacant vertices with at least k occupied neighbors become occupied. Criticality is for positive probability of eventual occupation of all vertices.

On Z the one-neighbor bootstrap threshold is zero, whereas the two-neighbor threshold is one because any initially vacant adjacent pair stays vacant. On the three-regular tree with threshold two, the final vacant set is the two-core of the initial vacant percolation. If its density q<=1/2, all vacant clusters are finite almost surely and leaf pruning empties them. If q>1/2, with positive probability a vertex has two surviving vacant branches, giving a bi-infinite vacant path that remains vacant. Hence the complete-occupation threshold is p=1/2.

An infinite bi-infinite path supplies a stable set since each vertex has two vacant neighbors. Finite trees have an exposed leaf and are exhausted by the pruning process. Critical Binomial(2,1/2) clusters die out.

This illustrates both the amenable endpoint behavior and a nonamenable interior threshold. It does not classify every generating set or every group.

Known for trees and networks with an infinite automorphism orbit. Distinct probability measures need not be singular in general.

For a fixed countable group action, two distinct invariant ergodic probability measures are mutually singular. In the Lebesgue decomposition of one relative to the other, the absolutely continuous part is invariant. Its density is invariant and hence constant under the second ergodic law; ergodicity of the first forces its absolutely continuous mass to be either zero or one. Nonzero overlap therefore forces equality.

The singular and absolutely continuous parts are preserved by the action by uniqueness of Lebesgue decomposition; this is the load-bearing invariance step.

This handles forest laws admitting such an ergodic common action. Arbitrary networks may lack it; two distinct probability laws need not be singular in general.

For a nondegenerate supercritical Galton-Watson law of mean m under the chapter's moment assumptions, must every consistent equivariant flow rule different almost surely from UNIF have boundary-measure Hausdorff dimension below log m almost surely?

The source proves a stationary-measure sufficient condition. Difference on a GW-null set is not an admissible counterexample.

For the AND/OR color construction of P0033, let K be the number of children of the parent color and choose uniformly among them. Conditional on root color zero, P(K=1,2,3)=(3/5,3/10,1/10); conditional on color one it is (3/10,3/5,1/10). The full conditional-child selection lemma implies these K variables are iid along the selected ray within each color class. Hence the local dimension is h_0=(3/10)log 2+(1/10)log 3 or h_1=(3/5)log 2+(1/10)log 3 by the strong law. Both are strictly less than log(12/5), the Galton-Watson dimension.

For color zero the unconditioned masses are .30 for two mixed children (K=1), .15 for two zero children (K=2), and .05 for three zero children (K=3); divide by color probability .5. For color one the corresponding masses are .15,.30,.05. Cylinder mass is exactly the product of reciprocal K values; Fubini transfers the ray statement to almost every tree and almost every flow ray.

This author-checked special construction supports dimension drop and is not a counterexample to the full question. It inherits the P0033 coloring proof and remains without independent review.

The two genuinely different height ensembles are conservatively grouped as one universality family. Integer heights have nearest-neighbor difference0 or2 and boundary values plus/minus1; real heights have difference at most1 and tuned boundary values plus/minus lambda.

The interval endpoints are the maximum of neighbor heights minus the slope bound and the minimum plus the bound. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.04673

Source statement date: 2026-08-24. Archived access: 2026-09-06T19:42:01Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Determine whether the chronological attachment map from a typical SLE2 path and the intersected Brownian loops to the resulting Brownian path has a unique preimage almost surely, or instead infinitely many.

Global noninjectivity is already noted by the authors. The question concerns typical fibers in the specified support. It is related to, but stronger than, recovering only the SLE path measurably.

Global noninjectivity cannot settle almost-sure invertibility. The map f:R->R with f(0)=f(1)=0 and f(x)=x otherwise is noninjective, yet it is injective off the two-point set and therefore injective on a full-measure set for a continuous input law. Conversely, x->|x| has two typical preimages for a symmetric continuous law.

A finite set has probability0 under an atomless law. For the absolute-value map, every y>0 has two preimages of equal conditional probability under a standard normal input.

One must exhibit an ambiguity mechanism occurring on a positive-probability or full-probability family of loop configurations. A deterministic exceptional pair or a measurable selection theorem does not do this.

The source explains that its planar deterministic continuity hypothesis fails in dimension3. A probabilistic continuity statement at typical configurations could still suffice.

A fixed planar circle intersecting a line in R^3 becomes disjoint from that line after an arbitrarily small translation in the perpendicular direction. For example, gamma is the x-axis segment[-2,2] and ell is the unit circle in the xy-plane; ell+(0,0,epsilon) avoids gamma for every epsilon nonzero while converging uniformly to ell.

Every point of the translated loop has z-coordinate epsilon and every point of gamma has z-coordinate0. At epsilon0 the circle meets gamma at(plus/minus1,0,0).

Attaching or omitting a loop of fixed diameter changes the resulting path macroscopically. Typical random intersections need a stability argument beyond deterministic uniform closeness; the example does not refute such an almost-sure statement.

# P0137  A loop-erased representation of a unit Brownian loop

Berestycki and Sauzedde: Brownian paths as loop-decorated SLEs,2026; Section7, SLE2 loop analogue

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.04673

Source statement date: 2026-08-24. Archived access: 2026-09-06T19:42:01Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Describe a unit Brownian loop as an SLE2-type loop decorated by an independent Brownian loop soup, with a precise law and chronology.

A closed loop has no distinguished endpoint ordering. Rooting conventions, duration conditioning, and the law of the proposed SLE loop must be fixed together.

Even in a finite closed walk, rooting before chronological loop erasure can discard all information: the standard loop erasure of a finite walk ending at its starting vertex is the single starting vertex. When the terminal return is processed, it erases the whole currently retained path.

The standard stack algorithm retains distinct vertices and, upon revisiting a vertex already on the stack, removes everything after its previous occurrence. The final return to the first vertex therefore leaves only that vertex.

A nontrivial loop analogue cannot simply apply the open-path loop-erasure algorithm to an arbitrarily rooted closed Brownian path. A cyclic or marked-edge construction and its resulting sampling bias remain to be established.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Prove appropriate Holder, p-variation, or rough-path continuity estimates for the chronological loop-attachment map, possibly restricted to the cusp conditions proposed by the authors.

The precise topology must include all necessary time and iterated-integral information. Continuity in the source's existing path topology does not imply continuity of rough-path lifts.

Concatenate m positively oriented circles of radius m^(-1/2), each based at0, over a unit time interval. Their sup norm tends to0 and, for p>2, their first-level p-variation is at most C_p*m^(1/p-1/2), which also tends to0. But their total signed area is m*pi*m^(-1)=pi.

Each circle contributes O(r^p) to the p-variation power, and splitting a partition at returns to0 changes the bound by only a p-dependent factor. Areas add over closed concatenated loops and equal pi*r^2 per circle.

This proves that first-level convergence alone cannot control the second iterated integral. It does not rule out continuity with properly enhanced input loops or the source's additional cusp restrictions.

Two-sided logarithmic bounds are weaker than convergence to constants. The positive-delta regime is the finite-variance degree regime; logarithmic-logarithmic formulas from negative delta do not apply.

Parameter regimes are one source problem, not separate corpus variants. Tightness and full-sequence convergence must be distinguished because graph distances are integer-valued.

If integer-valued X_n is centered by real c_n, every centered value lies in Z-c_n. Along a subsequence with fractional parts c_n tending to r, any weak limit is supported on Z-r. The source explicitly says the question concerns random fluctuations beyond the leading quantile-sum scale. Later leading-order weighted-distance results must not be mistaken for a complete centered limiting law.

For nonnegative weights, a path sum is at least its maximum edge, so the FPP distance dominates the minimax path value. The latter is exactly the smallest level t at which the two vertices are connected using edges of weight at most t. This follows by comparing the same path family under the two objectives.

The target is hopcount, not total weight or unweighted distance. Separate edge-weight laws may lead to different behaviors but are one classification problem.

If all weights lie in[a,b] with0<a<=b, the hopcount H of a minimizing path and graph distance d satisfy d<=H<=(b/a)d: a shortest unweighted path costs at most bd, whereas the chosen path costs at least aH. The known regular-graph constants use a branching-generation large-deviation calculation. Replacing the degree by its mean is not justified for extremes.

On a graph with maximum degree Delta, there are at most n*Delta*(Delta-1)^(k-1) oriented simple k-edge paths. With iid weights Y, the chance any such path has total weight at most t is at most this count times exp(a*t)*(E exp(-aY))^k for every a>0.

After the first edge there are at most Delta-1 nonbacktracking choices. Independence along a simple path and exponential Markov inequality bound its lower-tail cost. The union bound needs no independence between different paths.

# P0152  Kernel criteria for critical inhomogeneous random-graph universality

Van der Hofstad: Stochastic processes on random graphs, Saint-Flour2017; Open Problem4.5-4.6, PDF pp.222-223

https://www.win.tue.nl/~rhofstad/SaintFlour_SPoRG_fin_Saint_Flour.pdf

Source statement date: 2017-07-12. Archived access: 2026-09-06T19:31:10Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Characterize critical component universality for general inhomogeneous random-graph kernels, including the proposed role of the positive principal eigenfunction belonging to L3.

The general question and the eigenfunction criterion are grouped. Rank-one and finite-type theorems do not cover every irreducible unbounded kernel.

L3 integrability of the principal eigenfunction does not itself give a spectral gap. Partition[0,1] into blocks of masses p_i tending to0, choose epsilon_i>0 tending to0, and let m=sum p_i epsilon_i. On blocks i,j set kappa=(1-epsilon_i)1{i=j}/p_i+epsilon_i epsilon_j/m. This symmetric positive kernel has row integral1, so its principal eigenfunction is the constant1 in L3. For the centered indicator of block i, the Rayleigh quotient tends to1 as epsilon_i tends to0.

The row integral is1-epsilon_i+epsilon_i=1. The Dirichlet energy of the block indicator is at most p_i epsilon_i, while its centered L2 norm squared is p_i(1-p_i). Thus the spectral gap is at most epsilon_i/(1-p_i), tending to0. Positivity of the kernel makes the constant eigenfunction unique up to scale.

The example is an obstruction to using an unstated spectral-gap consequence of the conjectured criterion. It is not asserted to refute random-graph universality; the component scaling for this explicit kernel remains to be analyzed.

A high degree need not imply large escape capacity. Attach K leaves to a vertex v that has just one additional edge leading into a fixed transient infinite tree. Condition on the first step from v. Each leaf contributes0 to the sum of neighbor escape probabilities, and the one transient branch contributes at most1. This is the usual unit-conductance singleton capacity calculation.

Consequently, with iid continuous weights, the distribution of the unweighted MST geometry depends only on a uniform random edge ordering.

An iid continuous law gives no ties almost surely and every ordering has probability1/|E|!. The greedy cycle criterion depends only on the ordering, which independently verifies distributional invariance.

The remaining difficulty is the graph ensemble and the global near-critical component-merger geometry. Rank invariance does not establish tightness, scaling exponents, or the limiting tree.

The source contrasts this with taking temperature to0 at fixed n. Later random-regular metastability results are known; the full general configuration-model extension is retained.

A deterministic expansion condition gives an energy barrier. If every vertex set S of size at most n/2 has at least h|S| boundary edges, and the Hamiltonian is-J sum_edges sigma_u sigma_v-B sum_v sigma_v, then changing S from minus to plus costs2J|boundary S|-2B|S|, at least2(Jh-B)|S|. Every single-spin path from all minus to all plus crosses a set of size floor(n/2).

Each boundary edge changes its interaction contribution by2J and each flipped spin changes its field contribution by-2B. The number of plus spins changes by1 per step, forcing the intermediate set size.

A positive energy barrier is not by itself a fixed-temperature exit-time theorem because exponentially many configurations contribute entropy. One must compare beta times the barrier with entropy and control the metastable basin, with expansion estimates valid for the sampled graph.

Let G have odd n and edge expansion |boundary S|>=h|S| for all |S|<=n/2. Use H(sigma)=-J sum_edges sigma_u sigma_v-B sum_v sigma_v with J>0,B>=0,Jh>B, and Gibbs law pi proportional to exp(-beta H). Consider any reversible single-spin continuous-time chain with each individual spin-flip rate at most1. Put A={number of plus spins< n/2}. Global spin reversal maps A bijectively onto its complement and does not decrease Gibbs weight, so pi(A)<=1/2. An A-to-complement jump must start with(n-1)/2 plus spins, whose energy exceeds the all-minus energy by at least(Jh-B)(n-1). There are at most2^n such states and total exit rate at most n per state. Since pi(A) is at least the all-minus weight, the conductance Phi=Q(A,A-complement)/pi(A) is at most n*2^n*exp[-beta(Jh-B)(n-1)]. Starting with pi conditioned on A, the time-s law is bounded above by pi/pi(A), by Markov-kernel positivity and stationarity. Consequently the expected number of A-to-complement jumps by time t is at most t*Phi. The probability of still being in A at time t is at least1-t*Phi, giving total variation distance at least1/2-t*Phi. Convexity of total variation implies the same lower bound for the worst starting state. Therefore t_mix(1/4)>=1/(4*Phi), at least exp[beta(Jh-B)(n-1)]/(4*n*2^n). This is exponential in n when beta(Jh-B)>log2. The calculation accounts explicitly for entropy. It is a deterministic expansion-based mixing lower bound; it does not prove a metastable exit-time distribution, or expansion for every configuration-model degree law.

Boundary-layer counting and stationary domination give separate energy and time estimates.

No general random-graph expansion theorem or metastable exit-time distribution is proved.

Source statement date: 2018-03-23. Archived access: 2026-09-06T21:27:11Z.

Is the free additive convolution of two symmetric unimodal probability laws unimodal?

The older AIM free-analysis question is the same family and is not counted again. A semicircle factor and some freely infinitely divisible subclasses are established cases.

The classical proof by mixing symmetric unimodal components does not transfer by linearity: free convolution is not affine even on symmetric unimodal laws. Let mu=(delta_0+S(0,2))/2 and nu=S(0,1). The sixth moment of mu free-added to nu is67, whereas the mixture of the two component free convolutions has sixth moment70.

For mu, m2=1,m4=4,m6=20, so its free cumulants are k2=1,k4=2,k6=3. Adding nu changes k2 to2 only, giving m6=3+6*2*2+5*2^3=67. The affine mixture would be(S(0,1)+S(0,3))/2, with m6=(5+135)/2=70. Both mixture components and mu are symmetric unimodal.

This disproves a proposed proof mechanism, not the unimodality conjecture. The actual free convolution in this example is covered by the known semicircle-factor theorem.

# P0176  Existence of nontrivial freely strongly unimodal laws

Hasebe-Ueda: Large time unimodality, published version; Problem 3.11

https://alea.math.cnrs.fr/articles/v15/15-15.pdf

Source statement date: 2018-03-23. Archived access: 2026-09-06T21:27:11Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Does a non-point-mass law exist whose free additive convolution with every unimodal law is unimodal?

The source already excludes all nondegenerate finite-variance laws. The remaining possible examples must have infinite variance.

An explicit infinite-variance candidate also fails: the standard Cauchy law. Let nu=(1/20)*delta_0+(19/20)*Uniform[0,1000], a unimodal law with mode0. Cauchy free convolution equals classical convolution, whose density derivative, multiplied by pi, is -x/[10*(1+x^2)^2]+19/20000*[1/(1+x^2)-1/(1+(x-1000)^2)]. Its signs at0,1,250,1000 are respectively positive,negative,positive,negative, so the density has at least two peaks.

At1 the negative term is-1/40 and the positive term is less than19/40000. At250, writing A=62501 and B=562501, the derivative is -25/A^2+475/(A*B), positive because19*A>B. At1000 both displayed contributions are negative. The initial law has a single atom at its mode and a constant density to its right.

This gives a concrete Cauchy counterexample, consistent with the known strong-unimodality criterion, but does not exclude every infinite-variance law.

# P0177  Location of Brownian modes at large time

Hasebe-Ueda: Large time unimodality, published version; Problem 4.6

https://alea.math.cnrs.fr/articles/v15/15-15.pdf

Source statement date: 2018-03-23. Archived access: 2026-09-06T21:27:11Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Estimate the mode of classical Brownian motion started from a law with a finite exponential quadratic moment, and determine analogous estimates for free Brownian motion.

The source gives a growing interval of radius sqrt(t)/2 once unimodality holds. Classical and free versions of this mode-location request are grouped.

For the classical mode, let m be the initial mean and mu_k=E[(X-m)^k]. The source exponential-moment assumption yields the asymptotic expansion mode(t)=m-mu_3/(2*t)+(mu_5-6*mu_2*mu_3)/(8*t^2)+O(t^-3). In particular the mode tends to the initial mean, and the leading displacement has sign opposite the third central moment.

Set s=1/t and H(h,s)=E[(X-m-h)*exp(-s*(X-m-h)^2/2)]. The exponential quadratic moment makes H analytic near(0,0), with H_h=-1 there. The implicit function theorem gives h=a*s+b*s^2+O(s^3). Expanding H gives a=-mu_3/2 and b=mu_5/8-3*mu_2*mu_3/4. The associated density stationary point is a strict local maximum since H_h remains negative; the source large-time unimodality identifies it with the unique global mode.

This is an author-checked asymptotic partial answer, with no novelty claim. It does not provide a uniform explicit finite-time error constant or solve the free-Brownian half.

Use the published wording: classical convolution with classical stable laws, free convolution with free stable laws. The archived preprint wording differs. All stability indices are one source conjecture; the Cauchy case is already established.

A separated-atom counterexample of the source type cannot retain the critical moment while making its usual tail mechanism arbitrarily strong. If mu=sum_k w_k*delta_(a_k) and sum_k w_k*|a_k|^(2+alpha)<infinity, then w_k*|a_k|^(2+alpha) tends to0. # P0182  Strong convergence of high-dimensional representations of a fixed compact group

The strong convergence phenomenon,2025 survey; Section 6.3, p.66

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.00346

Source statement date: 2026-02-11. Archived access: 2026-09-06T20:51:12Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

For independent Haar elements of a fixed compact semisimple group, do their growing irreducible representations converge strongly to free Haar generators, starting with symmetric powers of SU(2)?

The source already establishes weak convergence in broad generality. The SU(2) test case and broader fixed-group question are one family.

The one-generator SU(2) case has an elementary complete answer. A Haar element has eigenvalues exp(plus/minus i*theta), with theta/pi irrational almost surely. Its N-th symmetric power has eigenvalues exp(i*(N-2k)*theta),0<=k<=N. These become dense on the unit circle, so every Laurent-polynomial norm converges to the supremum on the circle, the regular Z norm.

Irrational rotation makes the first N+1 multiples of2*theta asymptotically dense; multiplying the set by exp(i*N*theta) preserves its maximal circular gap. Uniform continuity then proves norm convergence for each Laurent polynomial. Geometric sums give convergence of every nonzero normalized trace moment to0.

For two or more independently sampled group elements, their representation eigenbases interact; the scalar circle-density argument no longer controls joint polynomial norms.

# P0184  Strong convergence of modular-group actions on finite projective lines

The strong convergence phenomenon,2025 survey; Section 6.4, p.67

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.00346

Source statement date: 2026-02-11. Archived access: 2026-09-06T20:51:12Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Does the PSL_2(Z) action on P^1(F_q), restricted to constants-orthogonal vectors, converge strongly to the regular group representation for every fixed tuple of integer matrices?

The diffusion-operator formulation and arbitrary-polynomial formulation are equivalent in the source and are counted once. Random homomorphisms from C2*C3 are a different model.

Weak convergence follows directly from fixed points. For a fixed nonidentity matrix X in PSL_2(Z), its fixed points on P^1(F_q) solve a projective quadratic equation. Except for finitely many primes where X becomes scalar, there are at most two fixed points. The normalized trace in the q-dimensional constants-orthogonal representation is therefore(fix(X)-1)/q, which tends to0.

For X represented by entries a,b,c,d, finite fixed points satisfy c*z^2+(d-a)*z-b=0, with the point at infinity handled projectively. A nonzero quadratic on the projective line has at most two zeros. Applying this to each word yields the regular trace moments. Faithfulness of the regular trace then gives the lower polynomial-norm bound by even moments.

Moment convergence gives no matching upper bound on operator norms; sparse exceptional eigenvalues remain the exact obstruction.

Removing the common constant vector of permutation matrices requires an explicit convention for deterministic matrices that do not preserve its orthogonal complement.

Naively compressing arbitrary deterministic matrices creates persistent defects. Let e be the normalized all-ones vector, P=I-ee*, and B a balanced diagonal matrix with entries plus/minus1. B strongly converges to the symmetric Bernoulli law. But on e-perp, PBP has the zero eigenvector Be, while all its other eigenvalues are plus/minus1. This is the literal general statement. It does not impose independent entries, independence of the matrix family, or a free limiting family. The narrower Ginibre-with-adjoints question is recorded as a remaining subclass, not counted again.

Complete candidate counterexample: rational clock/shift unitary pairs U_j,V_j approach an irrational rotation pair u,v strongly, while U_j^q=I and V_j^q=-I force det(zI-U_j-V_j)=z^q. The strong-convergence proof maps the simple irrational rotation algebra into the product of matrix algebras modulo norm-null sequences; injectivity gives every subsequential limsup polynomial norm and therefore the full limit. Normalized word traces are checked directly. The determinant calculation independently checks nilpotency. Full proof and all source dependencies are in the proof packet.

If nu is supported on a compact interval [alpha,beta] with 0<alpha<beta, must sigma_t free-multiplied by nu be log-unimodal for all sufficiently large times?

This asks whether the support-ratio restriction in Theorem 4.4 can be removed. Log-unimodality is unimodality after taking logarithms. The known positive theorem assumes a multiplicatively symmetric log-unimodal initial law; the question here allows non-log-unimodal initial laws.

Focused primary-source searches2026-09-06 found no verified later resolution. The arXiv page has one2020version and a2022journal reference. Author publication pages and Auer2026 concern related results, not a verified resolution here. Search absence is not current-open evidence.

Candidate negative answer: nu=(delta_(1/10)+delta_10)/2 yields failure of log-unimodality for every t>=5*pi. Set a=log10 and K_R(s)=1/[2*(cosh(s)-cosR)], F_R(u)=(K_R(u-a)+K_R(u+a))/2. Choose the unique R in[pi/2,pi) such that R/sinR=t/10. Lemma4.1 then asks whether F_R(u)=1/10 has at most two roots. But F_R(0)<=10/101<1/10, F_R(+-a)>=1/8>1/10, and F_R tends to0 at both infinities. Continuity gives four distinct roots, contradicting the necessary condition for log-unimodality.

The2026 phase-ordering paper still uses a quasi-polynomial plus-boundary estimate. Its biased random initialization theorem is not a worst-start plus-boundary polynomial bound. Critical and high-temperature established cases are not counted separately.

The direct disagreement coupling proves the high-temperature part. Write N=n^2 and c=4*tanh(beta). A single disagreement vanishes if its site is updated, while at most four neighboring updates create disagreement with probability at most tanh(beta). Thus the expected Hamming distance contracts by1-(1-c)/N when c<1. Iteration and the coupling inequality give tmix(1/4)<=N*log(4*N)/(1-c), up to integer rounding.

Changing one neighboring spin changes the heat-bath plus probability by at most tanh(beta), since the conditional probability is(1+tanh(h))/2. A path coupling along single-spin differences extends the bound to arbitrary initial pairs. Boundary sites have at most four variable neighbors, so the estimate remains valid with fixed plus boundary.

For4*tanh(beta)>=1 the coefficient ceases to contract. This is a failure of the local metric argument, not a lower bound showing slow mixing; the low-temperature interface regime remains unresolved here.

For the lower bound, magnetization from all plus has mean N*(1-1/N)^t and variance at most N, whereas stationary magnetization has variance N. Thus at t=(N/2)*(log N-C) the means are separated by order exp(C/2)*sqrt(N).

Does the shuffle that swaps the cyclically chosen position with a uniform random position have cutoff?

This is a time-inhomogeneous deck chain or a chain sampled by full sweeps. It differs from the cyclic adjacent-transposition shuffle, whose cutoff was proved by Nam-Nestoridi.

The one-card marginal admits an exact update that may identify candidate slow modes. If position i is chosen deterministically and the tracked-card probabilities are p_j, then p_i becomes1/N, while p_j becomes(1-1/N)*p_j+p_i/N for j different from i. Thus a centered vector z has new z_i=0 and new z_j=(1-1/N)*z_j+z_i/N. A sweep is the explicit product of these N linear maps.

If the card is at i it moves uniformly; if it is at j different from i, it stays unless the random partner is j. Summing the two cases gives the formula, which preserves the uniform distribution. Adding a deterministic phase as a state coordinate would give a periodic phase marginal and cannot justify ordinary mixing of the augmented chain.

The one-card product can supply lower-bound observables, but does not control correlations of all cards or produce a matching sharp upper bound for the full permutation.

Does proper-coloring Glauber dynamics mix in order N*log N whenever the color count exceeds Delta+2 on graphs of maximum degree Delta?

The book asks strictly more than Delta+2. Nearby formulations at Delta+2 are grouped. Later2026 results for high-girth graphs do not settle unrestricted graphs; vertex coloring is different from edge coloring.

The elementary Hamming path coupling stops at q>2*Delta. For configurations differing at one vertex, updating that vertex removes the disagreement. Updating one of its at most Delta neighbors creates disagreement with probability at most1/(q-Delta), by maximally coupling the two uniform available-color sets. Therefore E[H_next]<=1-1/N+Delta/[N*(q-Delta)], which contracts precisely when q>2*Delta.

The two available-color sets differ by at most one exchanged color, each has at least q-Delta elements, and their uniform laws have total variation at most1/(q-Delta). Iterating the path coupling yields an N*log N bound with constant proportional to(q-Delta)/(q-2*Delta).

Source statement date: author_page_accessed2026-09-06. Archived access: 2026-09-06T21:45:37Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

For an increasing subset V of the binary N-cube with at least half its vertices, is lazy induced-subgraph random-walk mixing always O(N*log N)?

The author page gives an O(N^3) theorem of Ding-Mossel and conjectures N*log N. This is the induced graph walk, whose stationary law is degree weighted, not automatically uniform.

Every such induced graph is connected and has diameter at most2*N: from any x in V one may flip zero coordinates upwards to the all-one vertex while remaining in V. Every vertex has degree at least the number of its zero coordinates, but the degrees need not be constant. For V equal to the cube with only the all-zero vertex removed, a unit-vector vertex has degree N-1 while a vertex of Hamming weight at least2 has degree N (for N>=3). Thus uniform stationarity is already false in an almost-full monotone set.

For an undirected graph, detailed balance holds with pi(x)=deg(x)/sum_y deg(y). On an edge between a unit vector and a weight-two vertex, a uniform law would have unequal transition flow1/[2*(N-1)] versus1/(2*N). The up-path connectivity argument is deterministic and uses only monotonicity.

Applying full-cube product Fourier estimates without correcting the stationary law is invalid. Diameter and volume alone give much weaker general bounds; the monotone geometry must control bottlenecks quantitatively.

https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Research/OP/cayley.html

Control the relaxation time of Metropolis random walk targeting the distribution of a Cayley walk at an independent geometric time; in particular, test monotonic decrease in the geometric parameter.

The source defines p in[0,1] but writes tau(infinity) in its proposed bounds; that reference parameter is undefined and is retained as a source ambiguity. The monotonicity question itself is precise. Its negative answer below is a partial answer to the grouped request for general bounds.

Monotone decrease is false already on the two-element Cayley group, with relaxation defined by1/(1-lambda_2). For the nonlazy base walk that flips states, mu_p=(1/(2-p),(1-p)/(2-p)), and its Metropolis matrix is[[p,1-p],[1,0]]. Its second eigenvalue is p-1, hence tau(p)=1/(2-p), which is strictly increasing. The same conclusion survives a lazy base walk: the base matrix has all entries1/2, mu_p=((1+p)/2,(1-p)/2), the Metropolis off-diagonal rates are(1-p)/(2*(1+p)) and1/2, and tau(p)=1+p.

For the flip walk, sum the geometric probabilities over even versus odd times. For the lazy base, X_0 is the identity and X_k is uniform for every k>=1. The nontrivial eigenvalue of a two-state stochastic matrix is1 minus the sum of its off-diagonal probabilities, giving both formulas directly. If laziness is imposed after forming the nonlazy Metropolis kernel, tau becomes2/(2-p), still increasing.

The literal monotonicity direction is refuted under the standard spectral-gap relaxation convention, but this does not answer the other universal-bound questions or resolve the source undefined tau(infinity). If relaxation meant inverse absolute gap for a nonlazy chain, that convention differs; the lazy example has nonnegative spectrum and removes that ambiguity. Prior-art status remains unverified.

# P0210  Martingales detectable by computationally practical stopping rules

Aldous open problems: Martingale for practical purposes; Problem and polynomial-constraint formulation

https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Research/OP/fields.html

Source statement date: undated author page;accessed2026-09-06. Archived access: 2026-09-06T22:04:12Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Give a useful probabilistic definition of martingale for practical purposes, or a tractable class defined by polynomially many stopping-time constraints.

The two formulations are grouped as one conceptual question. A complexity model and input representation are not specified by the source; no financial claim or backtest is involved.

Author-maintained page and relevant linked primary sources checked2026-09-06. Focused later-literature searches did not establish a complete resolution; current status remains unverified.

Any prescribed polynomial-size family of stopping tests can miss bounded conditional drift on an exponentially large history space. Reveal m fair bits by time m, set X_t=0 through time m and X_(m+1)=f(Y). For predetermined stopping rules T_j, each optional-mean constraint is the linear equation E[f(Y)*1_{T_j=m+1}]=0. If the number of tests plus the mean-zero condition is less than2^m, a nonzero f exists in their common nullspace. Rescale it to supnorm1. Then the process passes every supplied test but E[X_(m+1)|F_m]=f(Y) is nonzero.

The witness T*=m+1 on{f(Y)>0} and m otherwise is a stopping time and has E X_T*=E f_+>0. Predetermined test rules are functions of the revealed-bit history; their final-time continuation indicators do not depend on the unknown terminal value. The construction does not claim f or T* is computationally efficient.

A polynomial number of linear tests alone cannot reproduce the full martingale property. Selecting a useful computational subclass requires an explicit representation, complexity bound and error tolerance; the nullspace construction does not supply that theory.

Immediate parent-daughter returns renormalize the branching clock. For two independent simple walks started at neighboring sites in Z^3, their relative walk is a time change of simple walk. The probability they never meet is q=1-G(e,0)/G(0,0)=1/G(0,0), using G(0,0)=1+G(e,0) by the first-step identity and lattice symmetry. Thus a rare branch at rate beta produces a macroscopically surviving split at leading rate beta*q, rather than beta.

The equality of the two Green-function expressions follows from translation and reflection symmetry of all six neighbors. It concerns an isolated pair; the chance of interference by other particles has not been set to zero without justification.

A thinning heuristic suggests time scaling1/(beta*q), but a proof needs control of third-particle encounters, dependent return episodes and joint Palm genealogies. Stationary balance of split and merge counts does not imply independent Poisson clocks.

For the uniform model, sampling consistency gives an exact first-moment count: the expected number of agreeing k-subsets is binom(n,k)/(2k-3)!!. Thus P(C_n>=k) is at most this ratio. Stirling gives log of the ratio=k*[log n-2log k+2-log2]+o(k) when k is of order sqrt n. Consequently the elementary bound stops at order sqrt n, with threshold constant e/sqrt2.

The agreement probability is the collision probability of two uniform induced k-cladograms, exactly1/(2k-3)!!. Existence of a common larger subset implies existence of one of size k. The coalescent model has a nonuniform induced law, so its collision probability must instead be sum_T p_T^2; the uniform formula is not transferred to it.

First moments overcount many strongly overlapping agreeing subsets. They cannot reach the stronger known exponent bound or prove convergence of log E C_n/log n. The source centroid recursion constructs particular matches and is not automatically optimal.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Prove that the mean size of the largest common induced suborder of two independent uniform two-dimensional partial orders is asymptotic to c*n^(1/3), and determine c.

The source already gives order n^(1/3) upper and lower arguments. The calculation here makes a constant in its grid lower construction explicit; it is a rederivation of an established method, not resolution of the limit question.

Author-maintained page and relevant linked primary sources checked2026-09-06. Focused later-literature searches did not establish a complete resolution; current status remains unverified.

Partition each square into m-by-m cells, m=floor(n^(1/3)). Keep a label when its two points occupy the same cell, and retain it only if no other kept label shares that row or column. The retained labels have identical comparisons in both posets. For a fixed label the match probability is1/m^2; conditional on its cell, another label is a conflicting match with probability(2m-1)/m^4. Therefore the expected retained number is n/m^2*[1-(2m-1)/m^4]^(n-1), asymptotic to exp(-2)*n^(1/3).

Two retained labels have distinct row and column indices, so each of their coordinate orderings is determined by cell indices in both independent samples. Independence over labels gives the exact no-conflict probability. The bound is liminf E C_n/n^(1/3)>=exp(-2).

The isolated-cell matching discards many usable labels and supplies no matching upper constant. Optimizing a local grid construction does not establish existence of the global optimal limit.

A rigorous one-sided bound supports the balanced exponent when0<alpha<1 and beta>2alpha. Write d=beta/2-alpha>0. A union bound over influence disks gives area{I(y,t)>u}<=pi*c0^(2/beta)*u^(-2/beta)*M_t^(1-2alpha/beta)*t^(2alpha/beta), using concavity of the population power. Thus the conditional founding probability is at least1/[2*(1+K*t^alpha*M_t^d)], K=(2pi)^(beta/2)*c0. Put theta=(1-alpha)/(1+d) and m=floor(kappa*t^theta). Until M reaches m, each of the last floor(t/2) arrivals has founding chance at least p=1/[2*(1+K*t^alpha*m^d)]. Choose kappa small so this Bernoulli count has mean at least2m. A stopped coupling and Chernoff then give P(M_t<m)<=exp(-c*m) for large t.

The disk estimate is valid even at the square boundary because clipping only reduces area. Sum_i N_i^(2alpha/beta)<=M^(1-2alpha/beta)*t^(2alpha/beta). On the event M_t<m the threshold has never been reached, so domination by independent Bernoulli(p) increments throughout the half-interval is legitimate. The exponent identity theta*(1+d)=1-alpha makes the mean comparable to m.

This proves a lower city-count growth bound in the balanced regime, not the matching upper bound, comparable populations, unbalanced regime, or alpha1 logarithmic law. The upper bound requires control of spatial clustering and influence overlap that the union bound does not supply.

For a continuum Poisson process of intensity delta in[0,n]^2, rescaling coordinates by sqrt(delta) gives intensity1 in[0,n*sqrt(delta)]^2. Hence its minimum increasing-chain cover has the law U*(n*sqrt(delta),1), not U*(n/sqrt(delta),1). By the poset chain-cover/antichain relation it equals the longest decreasing subsequence, whose leading Poissonized Hammersley asymptotic is2m for a unit-intensity m-square. With delta=2*(1-p), dividing2*n*sqrt(delta) by2n recovers sqrt(2*(1-p)).

The expected number of Poisson points, delta*n^2, is invariant under the corrected scaling and would fail under the printed inverse scaling. Reflection converts decreasing to increasing subsequences, preserving the known leading constant2. These are checks of the continuum surrogate only.

One still needs a uniform comparison of the lattice closed-edge path-cover problem with the continuum antichain problem as n tends to infinity and p tends to1. The two corrected constants do not justify interchanging those limits.

Aldous open problems: One-dimensional drift-jump particle process; Problem,postedFebruary2018;1993notes Section4.1

https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Research/OP/left_Hamm.html

Source statement date: 2018-02. Archived access: 2026-09-06T22:10:42Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: attempted_unsolved

Give a useful explicit joint stationary law for the ordered particles which drift at speed x and jump left at rate1 Poisson space-time points.

The1993 notes already contain a patience-sorting representation and small-k calculations. The1999 paper Section5.2 uses the stationary process for limit theorems. Those established representations are not counted as newly solved open work.

Author-maintained page and relevant linked primary sources checked2026-09-06. Focused later-literature searches did not establish a complete resolution; current status remains unverified.

The established rank representation can be expanded into a convergent combinatorial density series. Let B=(1=b1<...<bk) be the limiting first-row labels of the insertion tableau, and let q_B be its probability. The first b=bk labels form a uniform permutation, so q_B=(1/b!)*sum over partitions lambda of b with first row length k of f^lambda times the number of standard tableaux of shape lambda with first row B. Independent unit-rate Poisson spacings then give density exp(-xk)*sum_B q_B*product_(i=2..k)[(x_i-x_(i-1))^(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)/(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)!].

Restriction of an insertion tableau to labels at most b is the tableau of the corresponding restricted subword. The last specified first-row entry b pins the first k labels, irrespective of later larger labels. Conditional on B, the Poisson arrival times have independent gamma increments, so every term is a normalized conditional density and nonnegative summation is valid. For k1 this gives Exp(1); known Poissonized LIS formulas give P(X2>x)=exp(-x)*I0(2sqrt(x)) and E X2=e.

This repackages a known representation into explicit but rapidly growing finite-tableau coefficients and an infinite sum. It does not establish a new tractable closed joint law or its novelty, and should not be promoted as a full solution to the source request.

Inscribed polygonal approximations to a semicircle are finite unions of straight segments with uniformly bounded length, while their limit is a smooth arc and is not a jagged route made of straight segments.

A compactness proof for length measures alone loses route labels, compatibility and the allowed-curve condition. One must choose a richer topology and prove closure or justify a relaxed model before claiming attainment.

Its local binomial point configuration converges in total variation to the corresponding rate1 Poisson configuration. The retained length is bounded by M, so its expectation converges. Summing disjoint unit-cell contributions and then taking k to infinity gives the Poisson local truncated expectation as a lower bound. Let M and then R increase: monotone convergence recovers the full sampled-network intensity ell.

Only a bounded endpoint region is used before taking k to infinity; its binomial count tends to a Poisson count and conditional positions have the same uniform law. Truncation avoids any unproved uniform-integrability step. Boundary cells are an asymptotically negligible fraction for fixed R.

A repair is to use w(t)=exp(-t)/(1+G(2t)), where G is the integrated diagonal heat trace: Fubini gives finite weighted row norm for almost every state.

Its projection has the coarse-chain path law. Any extra fine information can be represented by auxiliary conditional randomness in the coarse filtration, so this yields a randomized coarse stopping rule with stationary terminal law and the same expected duration. E_pi T0=a/[b(a+b)] and E_pi T1=b/[a(a+b)]. Substituting the two maxima into the harmonic mean gives the formula; differentiating(1+r)/(1+r^2) gives its exact maximum. Meeting occurs at the first jump of either distinct coordinate, total rate a+b.

The two-state calculation does not bound J/max E M on arbitrary chains. Rare spatial bottlenecks can affect stationary hitting times and two-particle meeting differently.

An elementary geometric lower bound comes from nearest-neighbor distances d_v: the ordered discovery walk has a departure from every vertex except its final one, and every such segment is at least d_v. Hence L_NUV>=sum_v d_v-max_v d_v. For unit-intensity planar Poisson points, Palm P(d_v>r)=exp(-pi*r^2), so E d_v=1/2. In the growing-square binomial version, the bulk expectation tends to1/2 and E max d_v=O(sqrt(log n)), yielding liminf E L_NUV/n>=1/2. In the complete graph with independent mean-n exponential edge lengths, the analogous bound gives liminf E L_NUV/n>=1.

The mean-field minimum at each vertex has mean n/(n-1), and a union bound gives expected maximum O(log n); independence between vertices is unnecessary for these expectation bounds. The Euclidean boundary affects only a vanishing bulk fraction for the lower bound, and the maximum estimate follows from empty-ball bounds.

These are lower constants only and may be weaker than established optimized-tour bounds. No subadditivity or stabilization argument proves convergence of the greedy length, and the source finite-size simulation constants are not theorem values.

Local finiteness implies a simple but weak path fact: if the infinite greedy walk is well-defined for all steps, then it eventually leaves every bounded ball, since it never revisits a chosen point and a bounded ball contains finitely many Poisson points. This does not imply it visited all those finitely many points before leaving. A deterministic locally finite configuration can have a path going to infinity while leaving an entire bounded subset untouched.

The distinction is between eventual departure and exhaustive visitation. The trivial upper bound on never-visited points is the Poisson count, asymptotic pi*r^2 almost surely, but no matching order or limiting density follows from self-avoidance.

The finite-window path law is sensitive to points outside the window. Identifying a translation-invariant limit of disjoint doubly infinite greedy paths, or quantitative exploration of missed points, remains the main obstruction.

# P0268  Abstract stochastic maximal regularity with non-small multiplicative noise

Agresti-Veraar: Nonlinear SPDEs and Maximal Regularity,2025 extended survey; Problem1,PDF91

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.18561

Source statement date: 2025-01-30. Archived access: 2026-09-06T23:40:06Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: unsolved

Find abstract operator conditions yielding stochastic maximal Lp regularity for (A,B), beyond the small-B perturbation theorem.

The source asks for a satisfactory structural criterion, rather than any sufficient condition: the small-norm sufficient condition is already established.

For simultaneously diagonal A and B on a Hilbert space, the homogeneous coordinate equation dX=-lambda*X dt+b*sqrt(lambda)*X dW gives E|X_t|^p=|X_0|^p exp{p*((p-1)*b^2/2-1)*lambda*t}. Thus positivity of A alone cannot supply a p-independent stochastic parabolicity condition. In the p=2 coercive regime b^2<2, applying Ito to ||A^(1/2)u||^2 yields control of E integral ||Au||^2 for additive input in D(A^(1/2)), after absorbing its cross term by Young inequality.

The moment identity follows both from the explicit stochastic exponential and from Ito applied to |X|^p. The coercive calculation uses the weighted norm A^(1/2)u, so it controls the full domain D(A), not merely the energy domain.

A criterion handling noncommuting A,B in Banach spaces must replace scalar coercivity and preserve the correct p-dependence. No such general criterion is proved here. Brzezniak-Veraar2012 already studies this p-dependence; the diagonal calculation is a known-model rederivation.

In the positive diagonal Hilbert model u_k(t)=integral_0^t exp[-lambda_k*(t-s)]g_k(s)dW_s, Ito isometry and Tonelli give E integral_0^T sum_k lambda_k^2 |u_k(t)|^2 dt <= (1/2) E integral_0^T sum_k lambda_k |g_k(s)|^2 ds. For q>2, the spatial Lq norm lies outside the quadratic sum and the Hilbert Fubini computation no longer identifies the necessary operator square-function property. Establishing an intrinsic equivalence, rather than a sufficient functional-calculus hypothesis, remains open here.

For spatially varying solutions, an L1 mass bound is not an L-infinity or high-Lp bound. Different species have different transport fields, so their sum does not satisfy a closed scalar advection-diffusion equation. For spatially varying coefficients the flow is not a translation, the transformed Laplacian has random variable coefficients, and the pressure projection no longer simply commutes. No general endpoint estimate or optimality proof is obtained. The2026 high-probability global result uses chosen noise and smoother initial spaces, so its abstract does not settle this question.

Source statement date: 2022-05-01. Archived access: 2026-09-07T00:46:33Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: unsolved

Does Ross workload monotonicity hold when the intensity is an arbitrary deterministic, possibly Boolean, function of a stationary doubly stochastically monotone CTMC?

An arbitrary image need not preserve the order on the original state space. Failure of a sufficient supermodular-order criterion is not itself failure of the workload assertion.

Consider the reversible birth-death chain on states1,2,3 with symmetric edge rates1 on1-2 and2 on2-3. It is doubly stochastically monotone. Its slow nonzero eigenvalue is3-sqrt(3), with eigenvector (1,sqrt(3)-2,1-sqrt(3)). The last two components have the same sign, so P_t(2,3)>1/3 for sufficiently large t. Label intensities f(1)=1,f(2)=0,f(3)=2. For g=1{f>=1},h=1{f>=2}, covariance at lag t is -(P_t(2,3)-1/3)/3<0. Hence the image process does not satisfy the supermodular time-slowing order, whose infinite-lag limit would require this covariance nonnegative.

The eigenvector sums to zero and direct multiplication by the symmetric generator gives eigenvalue -(3-sqrt3). The remaining nonzero mode decays at rate3+sqrt3, so it cannot cancel the eventual positive transition overshoot. The covariance formula uses g=1-1{X=2} and h=1{X=3}.

This blocks transferring the established sufficient supermodular-order argument through arbitrary f. It does not produce a queue-workload reversal. The source notes available nonsharp mixing-based rates. A meaningful minimax statement must specify covariate smoothness, response regularity, loss and reference measure; the entry records that unresolved model-class dependence rather than inventing a universal exponent.

In a location-family submodel Y=m(X)+Z with known noise law and a reference matching Z, the conditional transport map is T_x(u)=m(x)+u. Thus estimating the map under integrated squared error is at least as hard as estimating the regression function m: the map difference is exactly the shift-estimation error for every reference point u.

Integrating |T_hat_x(u)-T_x(u)|^2 in the shift submodel over a unit-mass reference measure gives |m_hat(x)-m(x)|^2. For an arbitrary map estimator, averaging T_hat_x(u)-u over the reference law produces an estimator of m(x), whose squared error is bounded by the map loss by Jensen. Thus a uniformly faster map estimator would imply an equally faster regression estimator on that submodel.

This reduction supplies a lower-bound route but no sharp rate for the general conditional map. One must combine covariate localization with the response-dimensional transport difficulty and prove a matching estimator under precisely specified regularity assumptions.

Its asymptotic covariance, when the joint CLT holds, is J*Sigma*J^T, where J is the Jacobian of this inversion and Sigma=sum over integer lags of Cov((1{W_0>0},W_0),(1{W_l>0},W_l)). For one class and attained service a, the index is the supremum over b>a of the Fbar-weighted average of h_c(y)=c(y)h(y) on [a,b]. For an absolutely continuous size law with hazard h, a job at attained service a allocated b servers completes at instantaneous rate h(a)*s(b), while its age advances at rate s(b). A formal controlled generator therefore has both an age-drift term s(b)*partial_a V and a completion term h(a)*s(b)*(V_after_departure-V). Maximizing the departure rate alone drops the learning and continuation terms. The common exponential case removes age learning but does not justify that omission for a general size law.

Conditional survival over work da is 1-h(a)*da+o(da); substituting da=s(b)*dt derives both generator terms from the same clock. A nonexponential two-point law instead requires jump boundary conditions, so the density formula is explicitly limited.

No solution of the infinite-state average-cost control equation or verification theorem is supplied.

Even with two jobs and no arrivals, continuation values change the allocation. Take four divisible servers and independent Exp(1) inherent job sizes. Use normalized concave speedups s1(b)=min(b,sqrt(b)) and s2(b)=min(b,b^(3/4)), including linear fractional-server behavior below one server. Allocate b to class one and 4-b to class two until the first completion, then all four to the survivor. Expected sum of completion times is V(b)=[2+s1(b)/(2*sqrt(2))+s2(4-b)/2]/[s1(b)+s2(4-b)]. Independently, the sign of the right derivative V_prime(1) is the sign of 3^(3/4)*(3/(2*sqrt(2))+1/2)-4, which is negative by the rational bounds 3^(3/4)<23/10 and 1/(2*sqrt(2))<9/25.

Harchol-Balter: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing; Section5; PDF16

https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~harchol/Papers/QUESTA21.pdf

Source statement date: 2021-01-27. Archived access: 2026-09-07T02:54:43Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: candidate_partial_counterexample

Determine how quickly the number k(n) of tasks per uniformly routed job can grow while the corresponding k(n) stationary queues remain asymptotically independent.

The source credits k=o(n^(1/4)); fixed-dimensional convergence alone does not answer the growing-dimensional question. Private author-only packet extends the credited coupling under exponential service. Later primary-source leads do not establish novelty.

Focused later-primary-source checks on 2026-09-07; offline concave scheduling, general FCFS threshold representation, SEK-SMOD and fork-join asymptotics credited. No present-openness certification.

A finite-horizon input coupling suggests a cubic collision scale. Fix k tagged servers. Jobs arrive at rate Lambda=lambda*n/k and choose a uniform k-subset. If N is the number of tagged servers hit by an arrival, E[N(N-1)]=k*(k-1)*k*(k-1)/(n*(n-1)). Remove arrivals that hit at least two tagged queues and restore their lost marginal rates by independent Poisson streams. A union bound on removed events and added events is at most (3/2)*Lambda*T*E[N(N-1)], hence at most 3*lambda*T*k*(k-1)^2/(2*(n-1)). The resulting streams are independent with the correct marginal rates. With independent task marks and queues initially empty, this also bounds total variation of their workload paths on [0,T]. Extending the credited source coupling to stationary starts gives TV<=2*k*r(T)+3*lambda*T*k*(k-1)^2/(2*(n-1)), where r(T) is the stationary marginal emptying tail. With independent exponential service of rate mu>lambda, a stopped generator calculation gives r(T)<=(1+sqrt(lambda/mu))*exp(-(sqrt(mu)-sqrt(lambda))^2*T). Taking T=2*log(n)/(sqrt(mu)-sqrt(lambda))^2 gives sufficient k=o((n/log(n))^(1/3)). A conditional polynomial tail r(T)<=C*T^(-p) gives sufficient exponent p/(3*p+1).

The hypergeometric factorial moment follows by summing ordered pairs of tagged-server indicators. On N>=2, both 1<=N(N-1)/2 and N<=N(N-1), giving the factor 3/2. Small subset enumeration checks the moment exactly. Separate exact checks cover 77 hypergeometric/restoration cases, 81 generator identities, nine geometric exponential moments and five polynomial balancing identities. The complete packet explicitly checks stationary coupling, marginal rate restoration, PASTA and heavy-traffic limits; these are author checks, not independent review.

Partial exponential-service sufficient regime only. No optimal threshold, boundary k of order n^(1/3), general-service improvement, correlated-mark result, uniform heavy-traffic result or novelty certification. The basic source coupling is credited.

The coordinate-diagonal case is a sum of binary entropies, whose second derivatives are -1/[q(1-q)]. There is also an explicit non-diagonal line: for Q(c)=[[1/2,c],[c,1/2]], |c|<1/2, the empty and doubleton probabilities are a=1/4-c^2 and the two singleton probabilities are b=1/4+c^2. Inclusion-exclusion gives p11=det(Q), p10=Q11-det(Q), p01=Q22-det(Q), p00=det(I-Q); these are a,b,b,a and sum to one. Differentiating H first gives 4*c*log(a/b), independently confirming the second derivative and its sign.

For a trigonometric polynomial f:T->[0,1] of degree m, is its stationary determinantal process an (m+1)-block factor of iid variables?

The source credits Broman2005 for degree one. A sublattice reduction proves new cases only when the lower-degree process already has a suitable block-factor construction; it is not an induction proving every even degree.

2026-09-07 bounded primary searches on entropy concavity, union coupling, block factors, Fuglede-Kadison domination and the linear distance bound. Known rank-one coupling and degree-one block-factor cases credited. No current-openness certificate.

Let f(theta)=g(k*theta). Its Fourier coefficients vanish at lags not divisible by k, so the determinantal kernel is block diagonal on the k residue classes. Determinant factorization proves that these restrictions are independent copies of P_g. If P_g can be represented as F(U_j,...,U_(j+r)) with iid U, define Y_i=F(U_i,U_(i+k),...,U_(i+r*k)). This is a shift-equivariant function of the window U_i,...,U_(i+r*k), so is an (r*k+1)-block factor. The residue-class families use disjoint iid coordinates and have the correct laws. In particular any single-harmonic symbol a+b*cos(k*theta)+c*sin(k*theta) with range in [0,1] inherits the known degree-one construction and is a (k+1)-block factor.

For cylinder events on distinct residue classes, all mixed kernel entries vanish and every required inclusion determinant factors. Inclusion-exclusion upgrades those identities to independence of the complete finite-dimensional distributions. The proposed coding depends only on positions at distances k, making its full window length exactly r*k+1.

General mixed-harmonic symbols remain untreated. Finite dependence by itself does not imply a block-factor representation.

# P0464  Geometric-mean product bounds for equivariant determinantal laws

Lyons: Determinantal probability, basic properties and conjectures, ICM 2014; Conjecture5.7; PDF23

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2707

Source statement date: 2014-06-10. Archived access: 2026-09-07T06:19:37Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: unsolved

For a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction Q on l2(Gamma), establish or refute the optimal stochastic product bounds with lower density FK(Q)=exp(tr log Q) and upper density 1-FK(I-Q).

The following classical conditioning argument gives weaker harmonic-mean bounds for finite groups and 0<Q<I. It is an author-checked supporting calculation, not a novelty claim or a solution of the geometric-mean conjecture.

2026-09-07 bounded primary searches on entropy concavity, union coupling, block factors, Fuglede-Kadison domination and the linear distance bound. Known rank-one coupling and degree-one block-factor cases credited. No current-openness certificate.

Put J=Q(I-Q)^(-1). Given the occupied set B outside e, the conditional odds of presence are s_B=J_ee-J_eB*(J_BB)^(-1)*J_Be. Schur-complement minimization makes s_B decrease as B increases. Its minimum is s_all=1/(J^(-1))ee=1/[(Q^(-1))ee-1]. The conditional probability, however, is s_all/(1+s_all)=1/(Q^(-1))ee. Equivariance makes (Q^(-1))ee=tr(Q^(-1)), with normalized trace, so this probability is the harmonic mean h of all eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Sequential sampling with common independent uniforms couples the process above iid Bernoulli(h), since every conditional probability given a partial reveal is also at least h. Applying the same argument to the complement gives the upper density 1-HM(I-Q). AM-GM applied to the reciprocals gives HM(Q)<=FK(Q), exposing the exact remaining gap.

For a scalar Q=qI, s_all=q/(1-q) but the conditional probability is q; this catches the odds/probability confusion in the incoming record. In a finite group, equal inverse diagonal entries average to the full matrix trace divided by |Gamma|, irrespective of whether the group is abelian. No sum over one-dimensional characters is substituted for the nonabelian spectrum.

No geometric-mean domination theorem or sharpness certificate. Numerical coupling feasibility is not exact proof, and the infinite-group extension of this particular calculation is not asserted.

# P0465  Linear coupling distance for noncommuting equivariant kernels

Lyons: Determinantal probability, basic properties and conjectures, ICM 2014; Section5.2 afterTheorem5.6; PDF23

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2707

Source statement date: 2014-06-10. Archived access: 2026-09-07T06:19:37Z.

Historical: source_says_open | Current: unverified | Result: unsolved

For sofic-group equivariant positive contractions Q,Qprime, does the invariant normalized Hamming coupling distance satisfy dbar(P_Q,P_Qprime)<=||Q-Qprime||_1 without a commutativity assumption?

The source states the linear bound for commuting pairs and a weaker power bound in general. We examine why the natural common-upper-kernel proof fails; the example is not a counterexample to the actual coupling inequality.

2026-09-07 bounded primary searches on entropy concavity, union coupling, block factors, Fuglede-Kadison domination and the linear distance bound. Known rank-one coupling and degree-one block-factor cases credited. No current-openness certificate.

Write D=Q-Qprime. A tempting common upper kernel is R=Qprime+Dplus=(Q+Qprime+|D|)/2. It dominates both in operator order, but need not be a contraction. In dimension two take Q=diag(1,0) and Qprime=(1/2)*[[1,1],[1,1]]. Then D^2=I/2 and |D|=I/sqrt(2). The largest eigenvalue of Q+Qprime is 1+1/sqrt(2), giving lambda_max(R)=1/2+1/sqrt(2)>1. Thus R is not an admissible determinantal kernel and one cannot apply monotone-coupling bounds through it. This same obstruction can be placed in the two-dimensional irreducible block of the right group algebra of S3, with zeros on the other blocks; the resulting operators commute with left translations but not with one another.

Direct multiplication gives D=[[1/2,-1/2],[-1/2,-1/2]] and D^2=I/2. The right regular representation of S3 contains its two-dimensional irreducible representation, and equivariant operators can independently specify a matrix in that block. On abelian groups the equivariant convolution algebra is commutative, so that setting cannot test this obstruction.

Failure of a common-upper-kernel construction does not refute the desired distance inequality. No claim of having executed a nonabelian coupling LP.
